passages.happening:
“Now Dinah, the daughter Leah had borne to Jacob, went out to visit the daughters of the land” (verse 1).

“When Shechem son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of the region, saw her, he took her and lay with her by force” (verse 2).

Afterward Shechem is drawn to her. He says he loves her and speaks to her tenderly (verse 3). He tells his father, “Get me this girl as a wife” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Dinah is Jacob's only daughter whose birth Genesis tells (30:21). She is Leah's child, so Simeon and Levi, who act later in this chapter, are her full brothers.

She goes out to visit the local women. That is all. The Hebrew carries no hint of blame for going out. The guilt of the next verse belongs to the man who acts.

Verse 2 says it plainly. Shechem sees her, takes her, and lies with her by force. He rapes her. He is the son of the local ruler, a man with power, and the verse names who he is before it names what he does.

A few scholars have asked whether the Hebrew words mean rape in the modern sense; Lyn Bechtel argued in a 1994 article that they need not. Most readers, and the BSB, read the verse as rape. On any reading the text does not soften it. Dinah is taken. Three times the chapter says he ‘defiled’ her (verses 5, 13, 27), a word for making unclean. And the narrator calls it ‘an outrage’ (verse 7).

Then comes the unsettling part. Shechem feels love for her and speaks kindly to her. His feelings may be real. But they come after the wrong, and they do not undo it. He does not ask Dinah anything. He tells his father to get her for him.

And notice whose voice is missing. Dinah never says one word in the whole chapter. We never learn what she felt, what she wanted, or what became of her. The silence is part of what the story shows.
passages.later:
The Bible tells a story like this one again. Amnon, a son of King David, rapes his half-sister Tamar. She pleads with him, “such a thing should never be done in Israel” (2 Samuel 13:12).

Israel's law says that when a woman is overpowered, she has done nothing wrong: “Do nothing to the young woman, because she has committed no sin worthy of death” (Deuteronomy 22:26). The guilt is the man's.
passages.asks: Dinah has no voice in her own story. Ask whose voices go unheard when harm is done in a family, a church or a town. Then ask how you could listen to them, and believe them.

passages.t: A father's silence, and a bargain
passages.happening:
“Jacob heard that Shechem had defiled his daughter Dinah, but since his sons were with his livestock in the field, he remained silent about it until they returned” (verse 5).

Shechem's father Hamor comes to speak with Jacob (verse 6). Jacob's sons come in from the field. “They were filled with grief and fury, because Shechem had committed an outrage in Israel by lying with Jacob's daughter” (verse 7).

Hamor makes an offer. “My son Shechem longs for your daughter. Please give her to him as his wife” (verse 8). He offers more: marry among us, settle among us, trade and buy land (verses 9-10).

Shechem himself says, “Demand a high dowry and an expensive gift, and I will give you whatever you ask” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Jacob hears, and he says nothing. The text gives a reason: his sons were away. But the silence stands out. It is his daughter, and the verse calls her that. He will not speak again until verse 30.

The brothers feel grief and fury. The narrator agrees with them that a great wrong has been done. ‘An outrage in Israel’ is a phrase later used for grave sexual crimes that tore at the life of God's people. Israel is still the name of one man here, so the phrase speaks with the voice of the people his family would become.

Now listen to Hamor. He speaks as if this were an ordinary marriage proposal. He never mentions what his son did. He offers a bride-price, a payment from the groom's family to the bride's family, which was normal in that world. Shechem offers any amount.

But there is something the brothers know and we learn later. Dinah is in Shechem's house while he bargains for her (verse 26). The offer of money is made while she is held.

Hamor also offers land and trade. Jacob's family could settle down and merge with Shechem's people. That would be a shortcut to the land God promised, on Canaanite terms, and it would dissolve the family the promise was for.
passages.later:
King David repeats Jacob's failure. After his son Amnon raped Tamar, the text says, “When King David heard all this, he was furious” (2 Samuel 13:21). But he did nothing. Her brother Absalom took revenge two years later (2 Samuel 13:22-29).

The Bible calls God's people to speak for those who cannot: “Open your mouth for those with no voice, for the cause of all the dispossessed” (Proverbs 31:8).
passages.asks: Jacob heard and stayed silent. Ask whether you have ever kept quiet about a wrong done to someone in your care, to keep the peace or to protect yourself. Then ask what speaking up would have cost, and what silence cost them.

passages.t: A sacred sign used as a trap
passages.happening:
“But because Shechem had defiled their sister Dinah, Jacob's sons answered him and his father Hamor deceitfully” (verse 13).

They say, “To give our sister to an uncircumcised man would be a disgrace to us” (verse 14). They will agree to the marriage on one condition: every man of the city must be circumcised (verses 15-17).

Hamor and Shechem agree. They go to the city gate and speak to the men of the city (verse 20). “These men are at peace with us,” they say (verse 21). And they add, “Will not their livestock, their possessions, and all their animals become ours?” (verse 23).

The men of the city listen, and every male is circumcised (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The narrator tells us before the brothers speak that they speak ‘deceitfully’. It is the same word Isaac used when Jacob stole his brother's blessing: “Your brother came deceitfully” (27:35). The deceiver's sons have learned his trade.

Circumcision is cutting away the foreskin of a man or boy. For Abraham's family it was the sign of God's covenant with them (chapter 17), the mark that they belonged to God. Here it is turned into bait. There is no word of God, faith or promise in the offer. The brothers know that grown men would be weak and in pain for days after the cut.

The city gate was where a town's men met to decide public matters. Watch how Hamor's speech changes there. To Jacob he spoke of marriage and peace. To his own men he adds the real attraction: Jacob's flocks and goods will become theirs.

So neither side is honest. The brothers plan murder under a religious condition. Hamor and Shechem plan to take Jacob's wealth under a marriage deal. And in the middle of the bargaining, Dinah is still held in Shechem's house.
passages.later: The prophets and apostles say the outward sign means nothing without a changed heart. Jeremiah warns of a day when God will punish “all who are circumcised yet uncircumcised” (Jeremiah 9:25), marked outwardly but not in heart. Paul writes, “circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the written code” (Romans 2:29).
passages.asks: The brothers used a holy sign as a weapon. Ask where religious words or practices can be used to trap, control or harm people. Then ask whether you have ever used God's name to cover a plan of your own.

passages.happening:
“Three days later, while they were still in pain, two of Jacob's sons (Dinah's brothers Simeon and Levi) took their swords, went into the unsuspecting city, and slaughtered every male” (verse 25).

They kill Hamor and Shechem, “took Dinah out of Shechem's house, and went away” (verse 26).

Jacob's other sons come and loot the city “because their sister had been defiled” (verse 27). They take the flocks and herds and everything else. “They carried off all their possessions and women and children, and they plundered everything in their houses” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
This is one of the darkest scenes in Genesis. God is not mentioned once in the whole chapter.

The brothers' anger has real grounds. Their sister was raped and was being held in her attacker's house. Their father did nothing. And they do bring Dinah home.

But look at what they do. They kill every man of a city for the crime of one. They do it by a lie, while the men lie helpless in pain. Then the other brothers take the women and children captive. The wrong done to one woman is answered by taking many women and children who had done nothing. Vengeance makes new victims.

The text does not approve. It tells the deed plainly and lets it be seen. Later, on his deathbed, Jacob will give his verdict on Simeon and Levi, and it is a curse on their anger.

Some later Jewish writings admired the brothers. The book of Judith, a Jewish book from about the second century BC, has its heroine pray to the God of her ancestor Simeon and praise his sword. Catholic and Orthodox Christians receive Judith as Scripture; Protestants place it among the Apocrypha, books they read but do not count as Scripture. Genesis itself does not share that admiration.
passages.later:
Jacob's last words to these two sons: “Simeon and Levi are brothers; their swords are weapons of violence” (Genesis 49:5). “Cursed be their anger, for it is strong, and their wrath, for it is cruel!” (Genesis 49:7).

Israel's law later said each person answers for his own wrong: “each is to die for his own sin” (Deuteronomy 24:16). And Paul writes, “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath” (Romans 12:19).
passages.asks: The brothers were right that a great wrong had been done, and wrong in what they did about it. Ask where anger at a real wrong has pushed you toward a new wrong. Then ask what justice looks like that does not make more victims.

passages.happening:
“Then Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, ‘You have brought trouble upon me by making me a stench to the Canaanites and Perizzites, the people of this land’” (verse 30). “We are few in number; if they unite against me and attack me, I and my household will be destroyed” (verse 30).

“But they replied, ‘Should he have treated our sister like a prostitute?’” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
Jacob speaks at last. Count the words ‘me’, ‘I’ and ‘my’ in his sentence. He speaks of his own danger and his own name. He does not mention Dinah. He does not mention the dead men, or the captured women and children, or God.

His fear is real. His family is small, and the towns around could unite and destroy them. But it is a father's failure that his first words are about himself.

The brothers answer with a question. They mean: should Shechem be allowed to treat our sister as a woman who could be bought? Their question has force. But it does not make the slaughter right.

And that is where the chapter ends. No one answers. Genesis lets both failures stand side by side: a father who counted only the cost to himself, and sons who counted no cost at all. The reader is left holding the question.

The chapter's answer comes later, in two places. In the next chapter God himself protects the family (35:5). And at the end of his life Jacob judges this deed (49:5-7).
passages.later:
God answers Jacob's fear in the next chapter: “a terror from God fell over the surrounding cities, so that they did not pursue Jacob's sons” (Genesis 35:5).

A psalm speaks to those who have been harmed and left without help: “The victim entrusts himself to You; You are the helper of the fatherless” (Psalm 10:14). Another says, “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18).
passages.hard:
Why is this story in the Bible at all? Not because it is an example to follow. Genesis tells the truth about the family God chose, and it does not hide what they did. It shows the violence done to a woman, and the violence done in her name. It makes no one a hero. Its silence about Dinah's own voice is part of what it shows us.

Nothing in this chapter teaches that a woman who has been raped should marry the man who did it, or make peace with him. Shechem's offer to marry her is part of the wrong the story exposes, not an answer to it. Nothing here is said against any people, then or now; the wrong belongs to the people who did it.

A word for anyone who has been sexually assaulted. This story does not call it right, and neither does the rest of the Bible. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. Where you were, what you wore, whether you fought back: none of it makes it your fault. Please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Jacob was silent when he should have spoken, and his sons were violent when they should have sought justice. Ask what a faithful answer to serious wrong looks like, between silence and revenge. Then ask who in your life needs you to stand with them.
